analysis.one_liner: Restricts retroactive credit card rate hikes, double-cycle billing, and surprise fees for cardholders.
analysis.headline: The Credit CARD Act passed the House 357-70 and the Senate 90-5 and was signed into law on May 22, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This law stops credit card companies from raising the interest rate on money a customer already owes except in a few defined situations, such as a payment more than 60 days late. It requires 45 days' written notice before rate or fee increases, ends billing tricks like charging interest on balances already paid off, and makes customers opt in before being charged over-the-limit fees. It also sets new rules for gift cards, restricts credit card marketing to college students, and requires companies to check a borrower's ability to repay before issuing a card.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly half of American households that carry credit card debt. Cardholders who pay on time keep their rate; anyone whose rate goes up gets 45 days' notice and the right to cancel and pay off at the old rate; payments above the minimum go to the highest-rate balance first; bills must arrive at least 21 days before the due date; gift cards can't expire in five years or quietly drain fees; and applicants under 21 need a cosigner or proof of income.

how_it_helps.text: Creditors may not raise the APR, fee, or finance charge on an existing balance except in four narrow cases: an expiring promotional period that was disclosed up front, an index change outside the creditor's control, a payment not received within 30 days after the due date, or completion of or failure to comply with a workout arrangement [S5].

Cardholders must get written notice at least 45 days before any rate increase or significant change in terms, and closing the account in response cannot trigger a default or accelerated repayment [S5].

The law bans double-cycle billing (finance charges based on balances from earlier cycles that were paid off), prohibits over-the-limit fees unless the consumer expressly opts in to such transactions, and limits such fees to once per billing cycle [S5].

Payments above the minimum must be applied first to the balance with the highest interest rate, and statements must be mailed at least 21 days before the due date, with the due date falling on the same day each month [S5].
Penalty fees must be reasonable and proportional to the violation, and creditors must consider a consumer's ability to repay before opening an account or raising a credit limit [S5].

Cardholders under 21 need a cosigner or proof of independent ability to repay, colleges must disclose card-issuer marketing deals, and gifts can no longer be offered to induce students to sign up on or near campus [S5].
The law bars dormancy and inactivity fees on gift cards unless disclosed and after 12 months of inactivity, and forbids selling gift cards with an expiration shorter than five years [S7].
Statements must show a 'minimum payment warning' table telling customers how many years and how much total cost paying only the minimum would take, plus a toll-free number for credit counseling [S7].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers and banks, which lose several of their most profitable practices: retroactive rate hikes on existing balances, double-cycle billing, unrequested over-limit fees, and unspecified penalty fees. Issuers can still charge high rates on new purchases and can raise rates in the four permitted situations, so some costs may be recovered through new-purchase pricing or reduced rewards. Gift card issuers lose dormancy fees and short expirations.

drawbacks.text: The law does not cap interest rates. Issuers may still charge high APRs on new purchases, and they may raise rates on existing balances in four permitted situations, including a payment more than 30 days late [S5].

Most provisions took effect nine months after enactment, and rate hikes were allowed in the interim window beginning 90 days after enactment if the issuer gave 45 days' written notice — giving issuers months to raise rates before the restrictions applied [S3].

The Senate added an unrelated rider, Section 512, allowing people to carry loaded firearms in national parks and wildlife refuges where state law permits; the House adopted it 279-147, with 145 of 255 voting House Democrats opposed [S5, S13].
Small business credit cards get none of these protections; the law only requires a Federal Reserve study of that market [S5].
70 House members voted against the bill; their side's motion to recommit would have added a trigger requiring further enactment steps before the law took effect [S11, S10].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and concrete: the practices banned — raising rates on money already borrowed, billing interest on balances already paid, and piling on unrequested over-limit fees — were ones cardholders could not avoid through shopping, because they applied retroactively. The main honest cost is that issuers lost a revenue stream and could respond by pricing new purchases higher or tightening credit, and the law itself requires the Federal Reserve to report on whether the act affected the cost and availability of credit [S5]. The nine-month delay and the unrelated gun rider are real flaws, but they do not undo the core protections.

outcome.mechanism: It moved fast: the House passed it 357-70 on April 30, the Senate amended it and passed it 90-5 on May 19, the House accepted the Senate version the next day, and the President signed it on May 22, 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the bill on January 22, 2009, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee [S1, S9].
The committee ordered the bill reported on April 22 by a vote of 48-19, and it was reported with amendments on April 27 [S9].
The House passed the bill 357-70 on April 30: 252 of 253 voting Democrats and 105 of 174 voting Republicans in favor; a Republican motion to recommit with instructions failed 164-263 [S11, S10].
The Senate passed its own amended version 90-5 on May 19 — 53 Democrats, 35 Republicans, and both independents in favor [S12].
The House accepted the Senate amendment in two votes on May 20, 361-64 on the main body and 279-147 on the firearms rider, with the rider passing mainly on Republican votes [S13, S14].
The President signed it on May 22, 2009, and it became Public Law 111-24 [S6, S9].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary cardholders came out ahead: they gained protections against retroactive rate increases and billing practices that had been at the issuer's discretion. Credit card issuers came out behind, losing some of their most profitable fee practices, though they kept the ability to set rates on new purchases.

sides.party_line_note: The bill passed with overwhelming support from both parties — 252-1 among voting House Democrats, 105-69 among voting House Republicans in the House, and 90-5 in the Senate; the sharpest partisan split came on the unrelated gun rider, which 174 of 178 voting Republicans backed and most Democrats opposed [S11, S12, S13].

industries.note: The law eliminates retroactive rate increases on existing balances, double-cycle billing, unrequested over-limit fees, and unspecified penalty fees — practices that generated revenue directly from cardholders' mistakes and confusion. Issuers keep the power to set rates on new purchases and to raise rates in four defined situations, so they remain the channel for consumer credit.

industries.industry: Gift card and prepaid card issuers
industries.note: The law bars dormancy, inactivity, and service fees unless disclosed and after a year of inactivity, and bans expirations shorter than five years — ending a revenue stream that came out of the value consumers had already paid for.

An unrelated rider added in the Senate allows carrying loaded firearms in national parks and wildlife refuges where state law permits, a win for gun-rights groups that had sought it; the House adopted it mainly on Republican votes over the objection of most Democrats.
